newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia-US summit will be fitness test for Yeltsin.
newsitem.headline: Russia-US summit will be fitness test for Yeltsin.

text.p: Boris Yeltsin plans to travel to Helsinki to meet U.S. President Bill Clinton next month, hoping to prove that, despite ill health, he is still a force to be reckoned with.

The trip, the Russian president's first international travel since June, is aimed as much at silencing his domestic critics as defending Russia's interests on the world stage, where it has been cornered by NATO's plans to take in former Warsaw Pact members.

The Kremlin leader has been secluded in government residences outside Moscow for most of the period since he was reelected in July, dogged first by heart problems and last month by a bout of double pneumonia.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac have beaten a path to his door, but the meetings have been low key and media coverage has been restricted.

Opposition politicians have seized on Yeltsin's absence from the Kremlin as a sign that he is no longer able to rule Russia, which they say is suffering from a damaging policy drift and needs a healthy leader at the helm.
Presidential officials have tried to silence the critics, repeating that Yeltsin is in control and recovering steadily and releasing brief television clips of his meetings with officials.
But travelling to meet Clinton on March 20 and 21 will be a much more convincing demonstration of the Kremlin leader's return to health, although it carries with it potential risks.

The Helsinki summit, announced by U.S. Vice President Al Gore in Washington on Friday, was transferred from the United States to Finland to put less of a strain on Yeltsin, who underwent a multiple heart bypass operation in November.

But even the short journey -- an hour's flight or an overnight train ride -- could set back Yeltsin's recovery. Just two weeks ago the 66-year-old Russian president was forced to cancel a planned visit to The Hague on doctors' orders.
Once in Finland, he faces the difficult task of trying to persuade Clinton, who like the rest of NATO is set on expanding the alliance, to take Russia's security concerns into account.

Moscow feels threatened by NATO's plan to invite some of its former Communist-era allies to join but Russian officials know there is little they can do to stop the expansion process -- expected to begin at a Madrid summit in July.

But Yeltsin's domestic reputation rests on his ability to show those back home who feel that Russia is letting itself be trodden on that he can extract some concessions from Moscow's erstwhile military foe.
